detail.abstract: Using data from the European Union Statistics on Income and Living Conditions (EU-SILC, 2011-2019), this paper examines the impact of Greece's economic adjustment programs-implemented through successive bailout agreements between 2010 and 2018-on intergenerational mobility. To address concerns related to co-residence selection, we incorporate information from the European Community Household Panel and estimate a two-sample two-stage least squares (TS2SLS) model. The empirical results indicate a substantial increase in intergenerational income elasticity toward the end of the bailout period, implying a decline in income mobility. This finding is robust to a wide range of checks, including alternative measures of income and mobility, the use of disaggregated income definitions and the presence of zero income. We further investigate potential mechanisms and provide evidence on the key channels through which the bailout programs contributed to reduced mobility. Overall, the analysis offers new insights into the evolution of income mobility in Greece during its post-crisis adjustment.

title: Bayesian Persuasion without Commitment

detail.title: Bayesian Persuasion without Commitment
detail.abstract: We introduce a model of persuasion in which a sender without any commitment power privately gathers information about an unknown state of the world and then chooses what to verifiably disclose to a receiver. The receiver does not know how many experiments the sender is able to run, and may therefore be uncertain as to whether the sender disclosed all of her information. Despite this challenge, we show that, under general conditions, the sender is able to achieve the same payoff as in the full-commitment Bayesian persuasion case.

title: American Bar Association Resolution 507 (2025) and Associated Report
affiliations: Temple University - James E. Beasley School of Law, Pace University - School of Law, University of Pittsburgh - School of Law, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Schnader Harrison Segal & Lewis

detail.title: American Bar Association Resolution 507 (2025) and Associated Report
detail.abstract:
This Resolution, adopted by the American Bar Association in August 2025, along with the accompanying Report urges the repeal of all taxes on menstrual products at every level of government and supports federal and international efforts to eliminate such taxation. 

The ABA’s Resolution 507 marks the first official stance by the nation’s largest professional association of lawyers on what is commonly known as the “tampon tax.” Grounded in principles of gender equity, tax fairness, and dignity, the accompanying Report makes the case that menstrual products are essential healthcare items and should not be taxed as luxury goods. The Report highlights the disparate impact of sales tax regimes on people who menstruate, particularly those already burdened by poverty and marginalization. Drawing on constitutional arguments, tax policy scholarship, and international comparisons, the Report situates menstrual equity as a legal and human rights issue. 

By recognizing tax policy as a vehicle for justice, the ABA affirms the responsibility of the legal profession to challenge structural inequities embedded in seemingly neutral laws. Resolution 507 provides a blueprint for lawyers, lawmakers, and advocates to advance tax justice as part of the broader movement for menstrual equity.

The Resolution was co-sponsored by (and benefited from the input of) the Section of Taxation, Section of State and Local Government Law, Section of Civil Rights and Social Justice, Section of International Law, Commission on Women in the Profession, Commission on Homelessness and Poverty, the Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion Center, and the Law Student Division. This Resolution and Report should be read in conjunction with the framing essay by Bridget J. Crawford, How the ABA Resolved to End the Tampon Tax, forthcoming in The Tax Lawyer (2026).

title: "More Work, Less Time for What We Will?" The Trade-Offs between Work and Non-Work Time in the US, 2003-2024, and their Implications for Worker Well-Being

detail.title: "More Work, Less Time for What We Will?" The Trade-Offs between Work and Non-Work Time in the US, 2003-2024, and their Implications for Worker Well-Being
detail.abstract: This article explores the association between the length of individuals' daily working time in the US and the amount of time they allocate toward non-work activities. To illustrate the trade-offs incurred by longer work hours, we use the Current Population Survey's American Time Use Survey, 2003-2024. We divide unpaid non-work time into leisure, household production, caregiving, volunteering, education, and sleep time. We find that each additional hour of work time is associated with a reduction of 15 minutes of housework, 5 minutes of caregiving, and 21 minutes of leisure. In addition to demonstrating differences in individuals' allocation of non-work time based on gender and household composition, we forward the current literature by revealing differences in time use based on race, education, and post-covid effects, raising questions for future research. We conclude by exploring the implications of these time allocation patterns and constraints for worker well-being and potential policy reforms.

title: After the U.S. Dollar Collapse: Rebuilding America's Financial System with a Multi-Metal Monetary System
affiliations: Faculty of Business Administration and Accountancy, Khon Kaen University

detail.title: After the U.S. Dollar Collapse: Rebuilding America's Financial System with a Multi-Metal Monetary System
detail.abstract: This study proposes a theoretical framework for reconstructing the U.S. monetary and financial system after a dollar collapse/reset. It outlines a three-tier model grounded in tangible assets with a regulatory, transparent oversight. Tier 1 establishes the U.S. Mint as the monetary base that issues a digital currency backed by a portfolio of metals. The nominal money supply target is maintained by daily, dynamically changing ratios that automatically respond to market conditions. Tier 2 comprises the U.S. Treasury, the Federal Reserve, and the banking system, which provide fiscal stability and credit intermediation without money creation. Tier 3 comprises the businesses, governments, and households. They interact through a digital ecosystem that promotes trust, inclusion, and transparency. The novel design integrates historical lessons from commodity-backed systems, modern digital finance, and the gold standard. A one-time debt jubilee transfers wealth to households, families, and small businesses, restoring solvency and narrowing the wealth gap between the haves and have-nots. The wealth transfer helps jump-start the consumer economy and rev up the nation's economic engine. The proposed system transforms money into an efficient medium of exchange and a stable store of value.

title: China's Approach to International AI Governance: Selective Shaping?
affiliations: Singapore Management University - Yong Pung How School of Law

detail.title: China's Approach to International AI Governance: Selective Shaping?
detail.abstract:
China is rapidly solidifying its position as a key actor in the development and governance of artificial intelligence (AI). Domestically, China is exploring a comprehensive and evolving regulatory framework. Internationally, China has transitioned from a passive recipient of external norms to a proactive norm-shaper, advancing its vision of AI governance through initiatives such as the Global AI Governance Initiative. This contrasts with its earlier accession to the World Trade Organization, when it adapted to pre-existing rules. As a leading AI power, China now influences governance practice at the international level.​

    This paper explores two important but underexplored questions: What is China’s approach to international AI governance? How to understand China’s approach? This paper argues that China pursues a strategy of selective shaping in international AI governance, resulting in a targeted reshaping of global order. By “uploading” China-proposed institutions and norms particularly in areas of strength, China leverages new initiatives and standards to shape the developing landscape of AI governance. Meanwhile, China’s approach also faces challenges such as normative ambiguity.

title: Digital Distance: The Shift from In-Person to Remote Socializing in India
affiliations: Apna.Co and Indian Institute of Management, Ahmedabad

detail.title: Digital Distance: The Shift from In-Person to Remote Socializing in India
detail.abstract: Using a 10% random sample of India's 2024 Time Use Survey, we document a substantial disparity in social interaction patterns: remote socializing (phone calls, messaging, digital communication) is approximately 40 times more prevalent than formal in-person community participation in time-use diaries. Daily participation in remote social activities stands at 1.55% (95% CI: 1.48-1.62%), while in-person community activities register at 0.04% (95% CI: 0.03-0.05%). This paper investigates demographic correlates of this pattern. We find that marriage is positively associated with remote socializing and negatively associated with in-person community participation, with these associations present for both men and women. Urban residence and higher education are also positively associated with remote social engagement. These findings document how India's social interaction patterns reflect both traditional social institutions (marriage, gender norms) and modern factors (urbanization, education, digital infrastructure). The patterns we identify have important implications for understanding contemporary social networks, though causal mechanisms require further investigation with longitudinal data. Our results contribute to understanding digital * Apna.co 1 transformation in a major developing economy where traditional community structures coexist with rapid technological adoption.

title: Baskets Full of Cash: Primary Market Frictions and the Performance of Active Bond ETFs
affiliations: Hong Kong University of Science & Technology (HKUST) - Department of Finance, The Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK) - CUHK Business School, Hong Kong University of Science & Technology (HKUST) - Department of Finance and Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST)

detail.title: Baskets Full of Cash: Primary Market Frictions and the Performance of Active Bond ETFs
detail.abstract: We find that active corporate bond ETFs earn lower net-of-fee alpha than comparable mutual funds, particularly among high-yield funds and even when comparing same-manager funds. We trace this performance gap to a friction inherent in the ETF structure: misaligned incentives between active managers and authorized participants (APs). Bonds received in kind from APs reflect dealer inventory pressures and subsequently earn lower long-horizon returns than bonds purchased directly by the same ETFs. Knowing this, active ETFs—unlike passive ETFs—rely predominantly on cash to settle creation and redemption, and trade directly in the bond market, much like mutual funds. We investigate the determinants of cash settlement and build a model that rationalizes the performance gap despite managers’ flexibility to use cash. Overall, these results suggest that the ETF structure introduces frictions to active bond funds, to which managers respond by using cash settlement as a partial remedy.

title: Structured Sentencing Algorithm for Ukraine
affiliations: National University "Odesa Law Academy"

detail.title: Structured Sentencing Algorithm for Ukraine

declarations.ethicsApproval: Disclaimer Text-generation software (AI Grok 5, ChatGPT 5, Perplexity, Grammarly) was used solely for editorial editing and style correction. All factual data have been personally verified and confirmed by the author. Responsibility for the content and accuracy of the legal analysis and recommendations rests entirely with the author

detail.abstract: This article presents the development of a structured sentencing algorithm for Ukraine that seeks to reconcile national principles of individualization with European standards of proportionality, while incorporating the autonomous interpretation of Article 7 of the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR). It identifies the limitations of applying a general sentencing formula to specialized liability regimes, including martial law, corruption offenses, traffic offenses under intoxication, military offenses, domestic violence, genocide, and crimes against humanity. A refined sentencing formula is proposed, incorporating corrective mechanisms and exceptions, informed by the conceptual principles of the Draft New Criminal Code of Ukraine. The article also emphasizes the importance of judicial reasoning, transparency, and predictability while safeguarding proportionality in high-risk legal contexts.

title: Who Gets the Callback? Generative Artificial Intelligence and Gender Bias
affiliations: Indian Institute of Technology Delhi and Argonne National Laboratory

detail.title: Who Gets the Callback? Generative Artificial Intelligence and Gender Bias
detail.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) become integrated into hiring workflows, they are actively shaping which candidates get shortlisted for jobs. While they promise efficiency and scalability, growing concerns have emerged about their potential to reinforce societal biases. Yet, how such biases manifest in modern LLMs across a wide range of occupations in realistic hiring scenarios remains unclear. Moreover, behavioural alignment of models through human feedback, aimed at improving helpfulness, may inadvertently shape model personality in ways that affect bias, but this relationship is poorly understood. Here, we present a large-scale audit of gender bias in LLM-based recruitment, using 332,044 real-world job descriptions together with simulated recruiter personas. We show that LLMs disproportionately favour men, particularly for higher-wage roles, and systematically associate specific skills, traits, and occupations with gender. A comprehensive linguistic analysis reveals that model recommendations closely mirror traditional gender stereotypes. Crucially, assigning a low-agreeableness persona reduces bias, suggesting that sycophancy plays a key role in reinforcing stereotypes. Moreover, controversial personas trigger internal model guardrails, leading to more cautious and less biased outputs. Our results highlight how AI-driven hiring may perpetuate existing labour market inequalities and have implications for fairness and diversity.

title: Who Owns Crypto in the Euro Area? Drivers of Crypto Adoption, Payment Use, and Its Interaction with Fiat Cash
affiliations: European Central Bank (ECB)

detail.title: Who Owns Crypto in the Euro Area? Drivers of Crypto Adoption, Payment Use, and Its Interaction with Fiat Cash
detail.abstract: Using a survey of 39,507 adults in 17 euro-area countries, I find that crypto-asset owners and the niche subgroup of payers have distinct profiles. Owners –⁠ typically younger, male, urban, and financially active –⁠ exhibit mixed payment preferences, valuing both cash-like privacy and card-like speed. In contrast, the small subset of crypto payers displays a strictly cash-centric profile, seeking to replicate features of physical cash-such as privacy and ease of use-in a digital form. Regarding the interaction with fiat currency, standard specifications show that holding cash reserves is positively associated with owning crypto, suggesting portfolio complementarity in normal times and challenging the view that early adopters reject cash. However, a multiple-instrument IV strategy exploiting pandemic-related payment shocks reveals a causal sign reversal: for compliers, adopting a precautionary cash buffer reduces the probability of crypto ownership when uncertainty rises. These findings (1) explain the wedge between high ownership and negligible payment usage (confined to a small portion of transactions of ∼1.4% of consumers), (2) suggest that crypto and cash function as portfolio complements in normal times but as substitutes under stress, consistent with a flight-to-safety dynamic, and (3) inform debates on financial regulation, public-private currency competition, CBDC design, and the persistent use of physical currency.

title: Agrarian Distress in India and its Relation to Global Economic Systems
affiliations: Oberoi International School (OGC)

detail.title: Agrarian Distress in India and its Relation to Global Economic Systems

declarations.ethicsApproval: Interviews were taken from primary sources. Verbal (recorded) consent was taken from participants before all three interviews were conducted.

detail.abstract:
India’s agrarian sector, which sustains nearly half the nation’s workforce, is in a state of profound crisis, marked by stagnating incomes, rampant indebtedness, and tragic rates of farmer suicides. Conventional economic diagnostics, however, consistently misapprehend the nature of this distress. This research paper argues that the prevailing Indian agrarian crisis is a direct consequence of the systemic shortcomings embedded in the one-size-fits-all economic models that are propagated and enforced by global institutions like the IMF and WTO. These models, which advocate for rapid liberalization, market-driven reforms, and a transition away from agricultural (rural) employment, are fundamentally ill-suited for an economy where agriculture functions as more than merely an economic activity. For India, agriculture is a critical social safety net and a cultural cornerstone. It’s the backbone of the nation’s economy: agriculture, with its allied sectors, is the largest source of livelihoods in India.


Moving beyond a superficial recap of the farmer protests, this paper employs a mixed-methods approach. It integrates macroeconomic data analysis with qualitative insights from primary-source interviews with key stakeholders, including Supreme Court Committee member Devinder Sharma and prominent farmer-leader Tejveer Singh. The analysis reveals a disconnect between theory and practice, and demonstrates how policies designed to encourage corporate entry and state withdrawal have instead heightened farmer precarity. This is further evidenced by various patterns of distress, such as the alarming rate of farmer suicides (which serve as a stark reminder of systemic failure). Figures from 2022 indicate that at least one farmer died by suicide every hour in India. Furthermore, statistical analysis of cost-price squeezes, stagnant household incomes, and volatile export performance illustrates how integration into global markets has subjected smallholders to heightened financial vulnerability without proportionate, or frankly, any measurable gains.


The paper culminates by presenting a critique of universal economic templates. It contends that the failure of these models lies in their inability to account for India’s unique socioeconomic background, where the prescribed path of development is structurally impossible. By contrasting the failed national policy paradigm with a context-sensitive, welfare-oriented alternative model exemplified by Kerala, this research makes a case for an indigenous economic framework. Such a framework must prioritize legal guarantees for minimum support prices, robust social security mechanisms, and strategic global integration (unlike the current wholesale path). Ultimately, this study aims to challenge the hegemony of decontextualized economic systems and advocate for development models that are both theoretically sound and ethically grounded in the specificities of places and people.

title: How Much Should CEOs, Doctors, and Unskilled Workers Make? An International Desire for Limited Inequality
affiliations: Yeshiva University

detail.title: How Much Should CEOs, Doctors, and Unskilled Workers Make? An International Desire for Limited Inequality

declarations.ethicsApproval: Data are from the International Social Survey Program, and participants could refuse to participate.

detail.abstract: What do people from different countries and social classes believe skilled and unskilled workers earn, and how does that compare to preferences about what those workers should earn? Nationally representative survey data from 29 countries were used to examine participants’ (N = 44,890) judgments of what chief executive officers (CEOs), general practice (GP) doctors and unskilled workers earn annually and, ideally, how much those different workers should earn. There was universal agreement that CEOs make too much compared to workers (a pay ratio of 9.09:1) than they ideally should (a ratio of 4.29:1). By contrast doctors were seen as making only slightly too much relative to workers (an estimated ratio of 3.5:1 vs. an ideal ratio of 3.0), and doctor vs. worker differences were not found in all countries. Direct pay estimates (rather than ratios) revealed that unskilled workers were universally seen as earning less than they should, CEOs as making too much, and doctors earning about what they should. Social class differences mostly involved perceptions of CEO pay. Overall, participants exhibited a desire for a limited range of income inequality – neither too high nor too low – and differentiated preferences regarding the pay for various categories of workers.

title: The Mc Kenna Options and British Financial Policy in the War of 1914 – 1918
affiliations: National Institute of Economic and Social Research

detail.title: The Mc Kenna Options and British Financial Policy in the War of 1914 – 1918
detail.abstract: When the British government issued a second War Loan in June 1915, the Chancellor of the Exchequer Reginald McKenna offered generous conversion options to holders of the first War Loan that had been issued the previous November, and to holders of Consols and some other government securities. He also promised that holders of the second War Loan would have free options to convert into any future War Loan. The Mc Kenna options were extensively exercised by investors, at a heavy cost to the government, and historians have criticised them as a needless waste of money. This paper argues that the criticisms are misplaced and that the options served two necessary purposes. First, the options to War Loan holders overcame the problems of price discovery in the bond market, which were caused by the uncertainties created by the war, and thereby enabled heavy government borrowing to be funded. Second, the options to holders of Consols alleviated the commercial banks' losses on government securities, which would otherwise have threatened financial stability.

title: Introducing Biosocial Psychoanalysis: A Unified Theory of Sexual Serial Homicide

detail.title: Introducing Biosocial Psychoanalysis: A Unified Theory of Sexual Serial Homicide
detail.abstract: This paper presents an integrative biopsychosocial psychoanalytic theory of sexual serial homicide that unifies biological, developmental, and psychodynamic research into a coherent explanatory model. Drawing on Freudian metapsychology and contemporary findings from neuroscience, attachment theory, trauma studies, and criminology, the framework explains sexual serial murder as the cumulative outcome of interacting vulnerabilities across the lifespan. Biological and neurodevelopmental factors-including genetic predispositions, endocrine anomalies, and traumatic brain injury-shape impulse control, affect regulation, and reward circuitry, creating a foundation for later risk. Developmental and relational disruptions such as insecure attachment, father absence, maternal enmeshment, humiliation, sexual precocity, and chronic trauma further compromise mentalization, internal object stability, and narcissistic integrity. These injuries activate psychodynamic processes, including splitting, repetition compulsion, nonprimary narcissism, sadism, and failures in symbolization, which consolidate into personality pathology and increasingly violent fantasy structures. The developmental case study of Bobby Joe Long illustrates how these multisystemic influences converge to fuse sexual, aggressive, and self-preservative drives and reorganize the ego around destructive aims. The paper introduces three integrative constructs-Drive Vector Addition, Object Possession, and the Ego-Accomplice-to articulate the metapsychological mechanisms by which this convergence produces sexualized homicidal behavior. By emphasizing interaction rather than single-cause explanations, the model offers a clarified theoretical foundation for future research, forensic formulation, and prevention efforts.

title: Financialization: How Fiscal Policy has Inflated Profits and Equity Valuations
affiliations: Research Affiliates, LLC and Research Affiliates, LLC

detail.title: Financialization: How Fiscal Policy has Inflated Profits and Equity Valuations
detail.abstract: This paper proposes a solution to an important financial market puzzle. Why have U.S. corporate profits and equity valuations reached historic highs despite a concurrent secular decline in net domestic investment? We argue that financialization of the economy created and sustains this divergence. First, fiscal deficits flow into profits by stimulating consumption. Second, distributions from those profits are recycled back into financial assets rather than into productive investment, thereby inflating valuation multiples. We conclude that financialization has likely produced a fragile market valuation that is fundamentally dependent on deficit spending and vulnerable to a severe correction when that fiscal support is inevitably withdrawn.

title: Measuring Healthcare Innovations Through Human Assigned Approach and Man-Machine Derived Approach: A Comparative Analysis Using Published Patents of India

detail.abstract: The intension of this paper is to judge whether machine learning algorithm can successfully extract the topic of a patent along the same line as human assigned patent class number serves and if so, whether title field alone or title and abstract both fields can extract the topics more precisely. The investigation was conducted using healthcare patents of India that were published between 2000 and 2022. WIPO's PATENTSCOPE database has been used and IPC classification scheme has been consulted. We found based on the IPC Class, Medicinal preparations characterised by special physical form, organic active ingredients, herbal drugs are a few important areas of healthcare innovation in India. Correspondingly, based on LDA model-based title analysis, Crystalline pharmaceutical composition of drugs, creams etc., Process of making herbal compositions are highly concentrated topics in title and Pharmaceutical preparation of solifenacin or a salt made by Heterocyclic compounds, Herbal extracted anti-viral agents/ Rotavirus vaccine composition are more crowded topics in abstract. Therefore, we found that LDA topic modelling can be successfully used to extract patent topics but the title field alone is insufficient to project the latent topics comprehensively. Therefore, title and abstract both fields should be used in visualizing latent topics for patent data and, still human expertise is needed for obtaining better projection of trends.

title: The Ownership Rule: A Gateway for Financial Crimes

detail.title: The Ownership Rule: A Gateway for Financial Crimes

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The purpose of writing this research paper is driven by a strong commitment to strengthening the resilience, transparency, and integrity of the financial system. My intention goes beyond academic analysis. It reflects a practical and urgent need to help financial industries and national economies protect themselves from money launderers, terrorist financiers, fraudsters, and other illicit actors who exploit structural weaknesses in regulatory frameworks. Financial crime damages societies, weakens institutions, distorts markets, and undermines trust in banking systems. When individuals can hide behind opaque ownership structures or manipulate regulatory gaps, the entire system becomes exposed to significant risks. This paper was written to address one of the most critical vulnerabilities: the global reliance on the 25% beneficial-ownership threshold. Although historically created to simplify compliance, this threshold has evolved into a major loophole that criminals use deliberately. By structuring ownership below reporting limits, they can avoid detection, bypass KYC controls, and infiltrate legitimate financial channels. My research examines how this threshold is misaligned with contemporary financial crime techniques and why it fails to identify the true controllers and decision-makers behind corporate entities. The goal of this research is to present a clear, evidence based argument for modernizing beneficial-ownership rules. The paper proposes moving toward full disclosure of all owners, controllers, senior executives, and account operators regardless of their percentage of ownership. Criminal influence is often exercised through positions of authority, nominee arrangements, or dispersed ownership structures, not necessarily through large equity stakes. Therefore, relying solely on percentage thresholds is no longer sufficient in today’s financial environment. The paper also emphasizes that banks and financial institutions should not allow companies to open or operate accounts unless they provide full and verified information on every relevant individual associated with the company. Each of these individuals should undergo complete KYC, identity verification, and inclusion in AML/CTF screening and monitoring systems. Strengthening transparency at onboarding is one of the most effective ways to prevent criminals from hiding behind layered legal structures, shell companies, or minority-ownership schemes designed to evade detection. My intention is to offer regulators, policymakers, and financial institutions a practical path toward closing a regulatory gap that has existed for decades. The recommendations included in this paper are designed to be operational, enforceable, and aligned with the capabilities offered by modern digital identity tools, data-matching technologies, and real-time screening systems. By updating disclosure requirements and improving verification standards, financial institutions can better detect suspicious patterns, identify hidden controllers, and prevent the misuse of corporate accounts. Ultimately, I wrote this paper to support the development of a cleaner and more transparent financial environment—one that is robust enough to resist infiltration by illicit actors and strong enough to uphold trust across economies. My objective is to contribute to ongoing international efforts to enhance financial-system integrity and protect societies from the significant harm caused by hidden ownership and unverified account operators. This research aims to help regulators strengthen oversight, support financial institutions in building more effective AML/CTF frameworks, and ensure that financial systems remain safe, resilient, and protected from those who seek to exploit them.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study does not involve patients or human participants. It is a policy-focused research paper based on regulatory analysis and publicly available information, so no ethics approval or participant consent is required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research has no external funder. It is a self-initiated effort, undertaken as a gesture of goodwill to support the financial industry in combating money laundering, terrorist financing, and economic crime, and reflects my commitment as a student of Risk and Compliance to contribute positively to humanity.

keywords: The Ownership Rule: A Gateway for Financial Crimes

detail.abstract:
This paper examines a critical structural weakness within global financial-transparency regimes: the widespread reliance on the 25 percent beneficial-ownership (BO) threshold. Originally designed to identify individuals exercising significant control over legal entities, the threshold has evolved into a predictable vulnerability that enables anonymity and facilitates illicit financial activity. Across major jurisdictions—including the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates illicit actors routinely exploit threshold-based rules through ownership fragmentation, nominee arrangements, and multilayered offshore structures, undermining supervisory visibility and regulatory effectiveness.

Drawing on consultations with senior U.S. legal practitioners, former SEC and FINRA officials, and banking-sector executives, the study demonstrates that financial institutions remain constrained by statutory definitions and cannot demand full ownership disclosure unless explicitly mandated. This limitation has produced systemic dependence on incomplete and often unverifiable BO information. The paper also evaluates the global impact of the 2025 FinCEN interim rule exempting U.S. domestic entities from BO reporting obligations, a development that conflicts with international standards and increases opportunities for regulatory arbitrage.

Using a multi-pillar analytical framework combining structural-vulnerability assessment, regulatory-influence theory, and behavioral analysis of illicit-finance tactics, the paper argues that the 25 percent rule is no longer fit for purpose. It concludes by proposing a comprehensive full-disclosure model requiring identification of all owners, controllers, and senior executives to strengthen global AML/CFT enforcement and enhance financial-system integrity.

title: Nonlinear Exchange Rate-Inflation Dynamics in Nigeria: Evidence from an ADL-STR-MIDAS Framework
affiliations: Central Bank of Nigeria, Central Bank of Nigeria and Central Bank of Nigeria

detail.title: Nonlinear Exchange Rate-Inflation Dynamics in Nigeria: Evidence from an ADL-STR-MIDAS Framework
detail.abstract: This study investigates the nonlinear and mixed-frequency dynamics of exchange rate passthrough (ERPT) to inflation in Nigeria using an integrated Autoregressive Distributed Lag-Smooth Transition Regression-Mixed Data Sampling (ADL-STR-MIDAS) framework. Utilising daily nominal exchange rate and crude oil price data combined with monthly inflation data for the period 2009-2024, the study examines how exchange rate shocks propagate through different macroeconomic regimes. Two nonlinear transition specifications-the Logistic STR (LSTR) and Exponential STR (ESTR) are estimated to capture asymmetric and symmetric adjustments, respectively. The empirical results provide strong evidence of nonlinear, regime-dependent ERPT: exchange rate depreciations have a significant and persistent positive effect on inflation, while the magnitude of pass-through declines during stable or appreciation regimes. Moreover, the LSTR specification provides a better fit, suggesting asymmetric transmission as inflation responds more strongly to depreciation shocks than to appreciation shocks. The findings underscore that Nigeria's inflation dynamics are shaped by both high-frequency exchange rate volatility and structural regime shifts. Policy implications highlight the importance of exchange rate stability, credible monetary policy, and coordinated fiscal discipline to moderate inflationary pressures in a volatile external environment.

title: Inflation Risk and Heterogeneous Trading Down

detail.title: Inflation Risk and Heterogeneous Trading Down
detail.abstract: I examine how households adjust the quality of their purchases in response to adverse economic shocks. Using household scanner data from Germany, I document heterogeneous responses across income levels. Higher-income households tend to reduce the quality of the goods they purchase, whereas lower-income households, who typically consume lower-quality goods, show a limited propensity to trade down, likely due to a limited ability to do so. To assess the equilibrium effects of an aggregate shift in demand toward lower-quality varieties, I implement a shift-share research design. This approach leverages two key components: (i) pre-determined spending shares on middle-quality varieties across the product space for a wide range of sociodemographic groups prior to the great financial crisis, and (ii) variation in population growth across these groups during the crisis. I find that a 1% aggregate demand shift toward lower-quality varieties following a recession raises the relative price of low-quality varieties by about 0.45% on average.

title: The Effect of AI on Retail Investor Behavior: Evidence from Account-Level Trading Data
affiliations: Haas School of Business - UC Berkeley, University of California, Irvine, University of California, Berkeley - Haas School of Business and University of Illinois Chicago

detail.title: The Effect of AI on Retail Investor Behavior: Evidence from Account-Level Trading Data
detail.abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) is rapidly emerging as a new type of information intermediary with the potential to reduce information processing costs for nonprofessional investors. In this study, we examine its impact on retail investor behavior utilizing account-level brokerage data across stocks, cryptocurrencies, ETFs, commodities, and currencies. Exploiting a temporary ban on ChatGPT in Italy as a plausibly exogenous shock to GenAI access, we find that during the ban, investors concentrate their trades in fewer assets, are less likely to initiate positions in new ones, and shift trading toward popular assets, consistent with increased processing costs. The effect is particularly evident for (i) stocks and cryptocurrencies, (ii) individuals facing higher processing costs, (iii) individuals more likely to adopt GenAI, (iv) hard-to-value stocks, and (v) around earnings announcements. Finally, the ban increases the correlation across holdings and raises portfolio volatility without affecting abnormal performance. Overall, the evidence indicates that GenAI enables broader retail trading activity by reducing information processing costs.

title: A Macroprudential Approach to Compound Climate Risks
affiliations: European Central Bank (ECB) and Council on Economic Policies

detail.title: A Macroprudential Approach to Compound Climate Risks
detail.abstract:
Climate-related shocks will not occur in isolation. Instead, they will unfold within an existing macro-financial environment, where their interaction may lead to compound losses. In such an environment, macroprudential buffers earmarked for specific risks have limitations, as they might not account for important correlations between climate-related shocks and other sources of financial vulnerability, nor for the extent to which climate-related shocks might compound existing challenges in the real economy and financial sector. In light of such complex challenges, this report investigates how a holistic approach can enhance the financial system’s ability to absorb compound shocks.

By exploring theoretical frameworks and practical approaches, the authors make the case for a consolidated macroprudential buffer framework to ensure the financial system’s resilience under increasingly complex and uncertain conditions.

title: Wage Bargaining Institutions, Technology Licensing, andWelfare
affiliations: and Aoyama Gakuin University

detail.title: Wage Bargaining Institutions, Technology Licensing, andWelfare
detail.abstract: This paper examines how wage bargaining institutions affect technology licensing and welfare in a unionized duopoly. We show that an outside innovator with a new cost-saving technology licenses it through a pure royalty (fixed-fee) contract rather than a two-part tariff under decentralized (centralized) bargaining. Under decentralized bargaining, adopting the technology raises wages, which incentivizes the innovator to mask the cost reduction through royalty licensing. Despite this production inefficiency, a lower wage pass-through rate under decentralized bargaining yields higher output and makes consumers, licensees, and the innovator better off, while labor unions benefit more under centralized bargaining.

title: Principles for Addressing Climate Systemic Risks with Capital Buffers
affiliations: Council on Economic Policies and Financial Services Agency of Japan (FSA)

detail.title: Principles for Addressing Climate Systemic Risks with Capital Buffers
detail.abstract:
This policy brief focuses on the potential of systemic capital buffers to address climate systemic risks. It argues that systemic capital buffers must simultaneously meet two distinctive but related objectives to address such risks adequately. First, they must ensure the robustness and resilience of the financial system when climate systemic risks materialise. Second, they must contribute to containing the buildup of these risks over time. Without the combination of these two objectives, supervisors would fall into an endless spiral in which a series of macroprudential measures continue failing at containing the buildup of systemic risks, and ever more macroprudential measures to maintain the robustness and resilience of the financial system would be required recurrently. In this context, the mitigation effect on risk buildup embedded in a macroprudential instrument is central to preventing supervisors from being trapped in such a hazardous spiral.

We propose four principles – absorption, prevention, individualisation, and recalibration – for a systemic capital buffer framework contributing to both objectives (resilience and mitigation). The combination of these principles would induce financial institutions to increase their robustness to climate systemic shocks and support their clients’ transition and adaptation efforts, thereby addressing the root cause of climate change and mitigating its systemic risks.

title: Production Inefficiency and Economic Inequality
affiliations: Bard College

detail.title: Production Inefficiency and Economic Inequality
detail.abstract:
Economic inequality remains one of the most explosive problems that human civilization has yet not solved. The persistence of inequality and the lack of solutions have led to a widespread conviction that the problem is in principle unsolvable. Dominant approaches that try to address the issue of economic inequality offer only palliatives that target the most egregious forms of inequality but not end it. The article challenges these approaches. It argues that the reason for their inability to solve the problem is their failure to understand its source. Current approaches toward inequality vary in their explanations of its origin. Some explanations point to conditions that were created by economic and technological advances, others point to private property and the rapacious nature of capitalism. The article argues that the main reason for the rise of inequality is economic inefficiency, i.e., the
failure to utilize all available resources for the purposes of production. The most important resource that is chronically underutilized is the creative capacity of human intellect. The article argues that the systematic underutilization of resources results in aggregation of wealth that is not used for productive purposes. Aggregation of wealth is the principal factor that makes inequality possible. The conclusion that follows from this analysis is that only elimination of
production inefficiency can put an end to inequality.
Economic production is an evolutionary phenomenon. The driving force of the evolution is the process of creation that generates new and increasingly more powerful levels of organization of reality, which is what the evolution is about. Universal inclusion is a distinct feature of this process. It uses all available resources to produce new levels of organization and advance the evolution. The utilization of all available resources is the essence of efficiency. Although
economic production originates in the evolution, it is chronically inefficient. The article explains the reason why economic production fails to replicate the efficiency inherent in the process of creation and the evolution.
From its analysis the article draws a conclusion that to achieve efficiency, economic production must use the process of creation as its main organizing principle. By replicating the efficiency of the process of creation and achieving full efficiency, economic production can eliminate inefficiency. By using all available resources, economic production can prevent the emergence of aggregations of wealth that makes inequality possible. To attain this goal, our economic
practice must use the process of creation as its main organizing principle. The article brings up the problem of anthropocentrism that prevents replication of the process of creation and is the main obstacle to obtaining full efficiency. The article also provides a general description of the main features that are to be embodied in the new practice that uses the process of creation as its main organizing principle.

title: Hunting Humans: The Paid Killers of Sarajevo and the Milan Investigation
affiliations: Lebanese University

detail.title: Hunting Humans: The Paid Killers of Sarajevo and the Milan Investigation
detail.abstract: In 2024, Milan prosecutors opened an investigation into Italian nationals who allegedly paid Bosnian Serb military personnel for opportunities to shoot civilians during the Siege of Sarajevo (1992-1996). This paper examines how these allegations transform our understanding of the siege from a military operation into a marketplace for recreational killing. Drawing on legal frameworks governing crimes against humanity, historical documentation, and psychological theories of moral disengagement, this analysis situates the alleged "sniper tourism" within transnational accountability structures. The investigation reveals how atrocity systems depend not only on direct perpetrators but also on networks of facilitators, financial transactions, and the systematic dehumanization of civilian populations. This case raises critical questions about individual responsibility, command accountability, and the role of international law in prosecuting citizens who commit crimes against humanity abroad.

title: Macroeconomic Effects of Carbon Pricing: The Role of Bank Credit
affiliations: Saint Mary’s University and Georgia State University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Macroeconomic Effects of Carbon Pricing: The Role of Bank Credit
detail.abstract: This paper quantifies the role of bank lending in shaping the short-run effects of climate policy on the economy. Using carbon price surprises from the European Union's Emissions Trading System, we document that higher carbon prices, while successfully reducing emissions, lead to lower economic activity, lower bank capital and higher credit spreads. We interpret these empirical facts through the lens of a dynamic stochastic general equilibrium model with polluting and non-polluting sectors, nominal price rigidities, and credit market frictions both in the financial and non-financial sectors. The model matches well the empirical impulse responses of key aggregates to a carbon policy shock. Counterfactual simulations suggest that the bank credit channel plays a quantitatively meaningful role in the transmission of carbon policy shocks. Finally, implications for the design of macroprudential and monetary policies are explored.

title: The European Trajectory of Egyptian Footballers: Performance Metrics and Contribution to National Team Longevity
affiliations: Graduate School of Business

detail.title: The European Trajectory of Egyptian Footballers: Performance Metrics and Contribution to National Team Longevity

keywords: Player Valuation Transfer Market Football Economics Club Spending Player Performance Squad Value

detail.abstract: This paper examines the defining force of African footballer migration to Europe, synthesizing the historical trajectory of talent flows with contemporary statistical analyses of player valuation, positional concentration, and career longevity. Historically, the movement began as early as the 1930s via French colonial networks, producing early superstars like Larbi Ben Barek. By the 1990s, the global impact of players such as George Weah, the sole African Ballon d'Or winner, established the continent as a premier source of elite talent. Four primary academy models-African, Afro-European, private, and non-affiliated-now underpin this robust export market, driven by encouraging scouting and investment. Extending the analysis to elite European competition, data on African players in the UEFA Champions League (UCL) underscores sustained, high-level influence, with figures like Mohamed Salah and Didier Drogba leading both all-time goalscoring Finally, our statistical modeling of "Egyptian player greatness" reinforces a deeply embedded bias in how career achievement is valued: while both international caps and years spent playing in Europe are significant predictors of a player's Greatness Score, the beta coefficient for Years in Europe (≈ 0.027) is nearly nine times larger than that for a single international cap (≈ 0.0031). This finding underscores that, within our model, longevity and stability in European leagues carry far greater weight than sustained involvement with the national team, even though Egypt proudly holds the record for the most Africa Cup of Nations titles. This bias is mirrored in public sentiment: after Egypt's friendly tournament in Al Ain in November 2025, head coach Hossam Hassan lamented that "we only have two real players in Europe, and a third who had limited playing time in France's Ligue 1 with Nantes." His comment reflects a prevailing assumption within Egyptian football discourse-that European-based experience is the ultimate benchmark of quality, sometimes even more so than domestic or continental success.

title: CEO Turnover and Big Bath Practices in Banking: Systemic Risk and Regulatory Capital
affiliations: Bangladesh Bank, Department of Banking and Finance and Monash University

detail.title: CEO Turnover and Big Bath Practices in Banking: Systemic Risk and Regulatory Capital
detail.abstract: We analyse CEO turnover in U.S. commercial banks to examine whether new CEOs increase discretionary accounting items. We consider pre-turnover attributes of performance, firm-specific risk and systemic risk, forced and voluntary CEO turnovers and bank regulatory capital. We show that new CEOs increase discretionary expenses in their first year, especially in low-performing or high-risk banks. This discretionary conduct amplified for banks with higher pre-turnover systemic risk, as well as forced turnovers. Furthermore, forced turnover combined with excess Tier 1 capital is associated with increased big bath practices. These practices do not improve short-term profitability; thus, earnings management is not the motivator - but often temporarily increase regulatory capital, suggesting motives such as truth-telling, risk management, and signalling.  Overall, the study highlights that big bath accounting is a strategic tool serving multiple objectives beyond earnings management, with implications for regulators, investors, and bank stability.

title: The 52-Week High Liquidity Mirage: How Behavioral Convergence Impairs Price Discovery
affiliations: The University of San Diego - Knauss School of Business, Macquarie University, Macquarie Business School, University of Sydney Business School - Discipline of Finance, University of Sydney Business School and University of San Diego

detail.title: The 52-Week High Liquidity Mirage: How Behavioral Convergence Impairs Price Discovery
detail.abstract: This study examines whether trading patterns at the 52-week high reflect investor disagreement or behavioral convergence. Using StockTwits sentiment, TAQ microstructure data, and machine-learning informed trading measures for S&P 500 stocks, we document agreement rather than disagreement. Belief dispersion falls while both retail and institutional investors symmetrically reduce trading and shift toward selling. Anchoring to the 52-week high generates a liquidity mirage, where effective spreads narrow and depth increases even as informed-trading intensity declines. Apparent liquidity masks weaker information incorporation, and stocks underperform momentum benchmarks by 30 basis points over five days.

title: Home-Country Geopolitical Risk and the Valuation of U.S. Foreign Private Issuers
affiliations: University of Memphis - School of Accountancy, Stevens Institute of Technology - School of Business, University of Wyoming and University of Wyoming

detail.title: Home-Country Geopolitical Risk and the Valuation of U.S. Foreign Private Issuers
detail.abstract: Geopolitical risk (GPR) can create uncertainty in capital markets, yet its implication for cross-listed firms is largely unknown. Using a matched sample of U.S. Foreign Private Issuers (FPIs) and non-FPI home-country peer firms, we examine whether home-country GPR associated with wars, terrorism, and international hostilities is a significant predictor of Tobin’s Q and FPI cross-list premiums. We show that both FPI and non-FPI valuations decline in response to increased GPR. However, FPIs experience significantly smaller valuation declines than their non-FPI peers, which has the effect of “widening” FPI cross-list premiums. To strengthen causal inference, we perform difference-in-difference (DiD) estimations around large spikes in home-country GPR, the start of the Crimea (2014), and Ukraine (2022) wars as natural experiments. Cross-list premiums rise more for FPIs from weak-governance or low-disclosure environments. Finally, we find that global GPR shocks are not associated with differential valuation declines between FPIs and their non-FPI home-country peers.

title: New Epistemic Zonal Indices for Early Detection of Financial Drift: A Comprehensive EZS Interpretation of Global Stability
affiliations: University of Warith Al-Anbiyaa

detail.title: New Epistemic Zonal Indices for Early Detection of Financial Drift: A Comprehensive EZS Interpretation of Global Stability
detail.abstract: Epistemic Zonal Statistics (EZS) introduces a cognitive-statistical framework in which stability, trust, and uncertainty are assessed through dynamic epistemic zones rather than fixed probability distributions. At the core of this framework is Trusted Zone Movement (TZM)-the directional drift of the system's trusted epistemic region in response to variance instability, noise accumulation, and shifts in zonal pressure. Unlike traditional financial statistics, which rely on volatility, correlation structures, or realised extreme events, EZS detects early signals of systemic fragility by monitoring the motion of trust itself. This commentary reexamines global epistemic indicators-including the Zonal Trust Coefficient (ZTC), Zonal Variance Instability Factor (ZVIF), and Zone Filling Ratio (ZFR)-and interprets contemporary financial conditions through the EZS perspective. The synthesized current evidence demonstrates a downward drift in TZM, signalling recessionary rather than inflationary pressure.

title: Deriving the Accounting Structure of Country-Specific SFC Models: A Step-by-Step Approach
affiliations: SOAS University of London, SOAS University of London and SOAS University of London

detail.title: Deriving the Accounting Structure of Country-Specific SFC Models: A Step-by-Step Approach
detail.abstract: Interest in country-specific stock-flow consistent (SFC) models has grown in recent years. These models are developed by either using a theoretical structure and calibrating it to a specific economy or by deriving the structure of the model using country-specific data. Although the second approach is arguably more suitable for replicating the unique features of economies, a barrier to the implementation of this approach has been the lack of clear guidance on how to derive accounting matrices that are consistent with the national accounting data of specific countries. In this paper, we address this by providing a step-by-step guide on how national accounting data can be used to derive these matrices. We explain in detail the decisions that researchers should take to develop accounting matrices whereby the model's stocks and flows are consistent with the actual national accounting items across time. A significant advantage of the proposed approach is that it allows researchers to derive data-consistent matrices, keeping the level of complexity at a minimum level. We illustrate how this approach can be used in practice using national accounting data for the UK and Portugal. We explain how the model structure derived via our approach is different from what a researcher would get by applying a theoretical model to these economies with a priori assumptions on which stocks and flows should be included in the model. We find significant differences between the UK and Portugal in terms of the intra-financial sector transactions and the stocks and flows related to pension funds. We explain why such differences matter for the results derived from country-specific SFC models.

title: From Sanctions to Price Surges: The Dynamics of Russia’s Import Prices
affiliations: Bank of Finland - Institute for Economies in Transition (BOFIT) and Bank of Finland - Institute for Economies in Transition (BOFIT)

detail.title: From Sanctions to Price Surges: The Dynamics of Russia’s Import Prices

publicationDetails.journalName: Bank of Finland Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: We examine impact of economic sanctions on Russian import prices using detailed data on other countries’ exports to Russia. We find that unit import prices of goods sanctioned by trading blocs such as the European Union have increased, often drastically, and even when imported to Russia from countries that have not formally imposed sanctions on Russia. For some countries, the unit export prices to Russia for non-sanctioned goods have also risen. These results strongly suggest that trade sanctions have been effective in limiting Russia’s access to sanctioned goods.

title: ASSESSING TRACE ELEMENTS AND RADIOLOGICAL RISKS AROUND URANIUM MINE TAILINGS: INSIGHTS FROM NAMBIA
affiliations: Namibia University of Science and Technology, Namibia University of Science and Technology, Namibia University of Science and Technology, Namibia University of Science and Technology and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: ASSESSING TRACE ELEMENTS AND RADIOLOGICAL RISKS AROUND URANIUM MINE TAILINGS: INSIGHTS FROM NAMBIA
detail.abstract: Groundwater contamination by trace metals and radionuclides near uranium mining sites poses significant environmental and public health risks.  This study assessed groundwater quality at two uranium mines in Namibia, a legacy operation active since 1976, and a recently developed mine commissioned in 2016, to evaluate spatial variations in trace element concentrations and radiological hazards.  Sixteen boreholes (eight per mine) located near tailings storage facilities were sampled for arsenic, cadmium, lead, uranium, and naturally occurring radionuclides (²²⁶Ra, ²³²Th, ⁴⁰K). Descriptive statistics, two-sample t-tests, and radiological hazard indices were applied to compare contamination levels against the World Health Organisation (2017) and Namibian potable water quality standards.  Groundwater from the oldest mine exhibited consistently elevated arsenic, cadmium, lead, and uranium concentrations, with all boreholes exceeding national and international guideline values.  The newest mine showed more heterogeneous contamination patterns, with certain hotspots, most notably borehole GW31, recording extremely high uranium concentrations (6700 µg/L). Statistical comparisons revealed significant differences in cadmium concentrations between the two sites (p = 0.01), while arsenic, lead, and uranium did not differ significantly.  Radionuclide activity was dominated by ⁴⁰K, and all calculated radiological hazard indices remained below the recommended safety threshold of 370 Bq/L, indicating limited radiological risk from groundwater ingestion.  Overall, the findings demonstrate persistent groundwater contamination associated with both legacy and modern uranium mining operations.  The study underscores the necessity for enhanced site-specific monitoring, stringent regulatory oversight, and targeted remediation interventions to safeguard groundwater resources and mitigate risks to surrounding communities.

title: Unconditional Cash Transfers and Early Child Maltreatment
affiliations: University of Michigan School of Social Work, Duke University, ,  and Wayne State University

detail.title: Unconditional Cash Transfers and Early Child Maltreatment
detail.abstract: BackgroundNewborns are at the greatest risk of maltreatment. Governments are experimenting with unconditional cash transfers to strengthen families and decrease the risk of child abuse and neglect.ObjectiveThe purpose of this study was to determine if unconditional cash transfers decreased contact with child welfare and substantiated reports of maltreatment early in life.  Participants and SettingThe sample included all births from 2019 through 2024 across the 64 most populous cities in Michigan, of which only Flint implemented the cash transfer program. The birth data were supplemented with city-level demographic characteristics obtained from the American Community Survey. Child welfare data were obtained from the Michigan Department of Health and Human Services.MethodsSynthetic control method (SCM) was used to construct a synthetic version of Flint, a weighted average of the 63 untreated cities, which approximates Flint’s pre-treatment trajectory in both outcomes and relevant predictors. SCM relies on the notion that a weighted combination of control units may estimate the treated unit better than any single untreated unit.ResultsEstimates indicate no differences in overall referrals to child protection and no differences in substantiated reports of maltreatment. These estimates are consistent for both abuse and neglect complaints.ConclusionsThe findings indicate there is no evidence that unconditional cash transfers totaling $1500 at mid pregnancy and $500 per month for 12 months affect contact with child protection or substantiated allegations of maltreatment within the first six months of life.

title: Banks vs. firms: who benefits from credit guarantees?
affiliations: Universitat Pompeu Fabra (UPF) - Centre de Recerca en Economia Internacional (CREI), Banco de España and

detail.title: Banks vs. firms: who benefits from credit guarantees?

publicationDetails.detailsText: Banco de Espana Working Paper No. 2523
publicationDetails.journalName: Banco de Espana Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Governments often support private credit with guarantee schemes, compensating lenders for borrower defaults. Such schemes typically rely on banks allocating guarantees among borrowers, but how banks do so is not well understood. We study this in an economy where entrepreneurial effort, crucial for efficiency, is not contractible, creating a debt overhang problem. Credit guarantees can boost efficiency only if they lower repayment obligations, but their allocation by banks is subject to two distorsions. First, insofar as guarantees are scarce, banks extract rents from all allocated guarantees. Second, banks tilt the allocation of guarantees towards their less productive and highly-indebted borrowers, from whom they can extract even larger rents. Our findings align with evidence from guarantees granted in Spain after the COVID-19 pandemic.

title: What is an Agent?  A Conceptual Primer and History of Agents and Agentic AI
affiliations: 273 Ventures, 273 Ventures and Illinois Tech - Chicago Kent College of Law

detail.title: What is an Agent?  A Conceptual Primer and History of Agents and Agentic AI
detail.abstract:
This chapter addresses the need for definitional clarity regarding "agents" and "agentic AI" amid widespread confusion in industry and academia. Drawing upon nearly a century of scholarship across eight disciplines—including philosophy, law, economics, cognitive science, and computer science—we offer a comprehensive framework for identifying and evaluating agentic systems.

Synthesizing work from Anscombe to recent advances in Agentic AI, we propose a three-level hierarchy of agency: Level 1 (Agent) is defined by the minimal properties of Goal, Perception, and Action (GPA); Level 2 (Agentic System) adds the operational properties of Iteration, Adaptation, and Termination (IAT), implemented through traditional algorithms; and Level 3 (Agentic AI) fulfills these six properties using AI or large language models (LLMs) for planning and orchestration.

Beyond theoretical definitions, we provide a practical evaluation rubric to help practitioners distinguish genuine agentic systems from sophisticated tools or single-shot chatbots. The analysis explores critical dimensions, such as the autonomy spectrum and entity frames, to clarify the boundaries between delegated proxies and self-directed entities. Finally, the chapter outlines essential safeguards for professional deployment in high-stakes domains like law and finance, including attribution, provenance, escalation protocols, and confidentiality controls.

title: The Curvature of Catastrophe: Collective Action under Tipping Risk
affiliations: Miami University - Department of Economics

detail.title: The Curvature of Catastrophe: Collective Action under Tipping Risk
detail.abstract: I study how nonlinear tipping risks affect collective action and its stability. In a dynamic non-cooperative game, agents choose costly prevention efforts that affect the probability of a catastrophic tipping event. The hazard’s curvature determines incentives: convex hazards make actions strategic substitutes and sustain free riding, while concave hazards create complements and amplify effort. I find that tipping risk encourages stronger collective action but can generate multiple steady states. When complementarity becomes strong under high but flattening risk, small shifts in effort are amplified through strategic responses, generating oscillations between high and low effort and thereby cycles of action and inaction. Tipping risk thus incentivizes collective action yet can also destabilize it.

title: Machine Learning Framework for Early Detection of Polio Outbreaks From Acute Flaccid Paralysis Surveillance Data

detail.title: Machine Learning Framework for Early Detection of Polio Outbreaks From Acute Flaccid Paralysis Surveillance Data

declarations.funderStatement: This research is funded by Canada’s International Development Research Centre (IDRC) and the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) (Grant No. 110554-001). We also acknowledge support from IDRC (Grant No. 109981).

detail.abstract: Poliomyelitis remains a global public health concern despite remarkable progress toward eradication. The continued circulation of vaccine-derived polioviruses underscores the need for enhanced surveillance systems capable of early detection and rapid response. Acute Flaccid Paralysis (AFP) surveillance, a key component of the polio eradication, plays a vital role in detecting poliovirus transmission but is often limited by delays in data collection, analytical capacity, and fragmented reporting structures. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) offer opportunities to address these challenges by improving data analysis, outbreak prediction, and decision-making. This study developed an AI-based predictive framework that utilizes AFP surveillance data to improve early polio outbreak detection. The dataset used to train the AI models integrates geographical, vaccination, clinical, and laboratory variables to capture the multifactorial determinants of poliovirus transmission. Ten machine learning algorithms representing tree-based, probabilistic, and neural approaches along with their ensembles were developed and compared. Among them, the CatBoost-based model achieved the highest performance, with an accuracy of 92.22% and an area under operating curve of 0.99, surpassing both standalone and ensemble models. Model interpretability analyses using Shapley Additive Explanations and Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations identified body temperature, fatigue, and sore throat as the most influential predictors in suspected cases, consistent with early clinical indicators of poliovirus infection. The proposed machine learning framework demonstrates the value of integrating explainable AI into routine AFP surveillance to enhance outbreak prediction, support timely interventions, and strengthen global efforts toward sustainable poliomyelitis eradication.

title: Convivencia of the Third Kind: The Rise of Rights of Nature and Life Balance Under the Cupola Called Earth
affiliations: Loyola University New Orleans College of Law

detail.title: Convivencia of the Third Kind: The Rise of Rights of Nature and Life Balance Under the Cupola Called Earth

publicationDetails.detailsText: Loyola University New Orleans College of Law Research Paper No. 2025-11
publicationDetails.journalName: Loyola University New Orleans College of Law Legal Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Convivencia - a term that translates to “living together” - is a concept that legal scholars have applied to the effort to develop a cosmopolitan jurisprudence that transcends the envelope of the nation state in the pursuit of ensuring humanity’s survival.

This article applies the concept of Convivencia to the debate about Rights of Nature when it comes to the future of our common home. Recognizing that nature is the indispensable enabler of life on the planet, the conferral of subjective rights upon nature at large or specific ecosystems promises a new jurisprudential paradigm for the protection, conservation, and recovery of all life systems. According to Rights of Nature advocates, the primacy of anthropocentrism—which sees nature merely as the object of human exploitation for the benefit of humanity’s economic development and technological progress—is woefully outdated when it comes to confronting the interlocking planetary crises embodied by climate change and species loss. These voices therefore urge jurisdictions across the world to shift the focus from human-nature binaries toward a more eco-centric world picture—one that has been associated with nature-rich locales and indigenous peoples’ spiritual concepts about the universe.

While Rights of Nature have offered tailored solutions for specific locations and particular communities across the world, these rights may not necessarily be a good fit for Western liberal democracies with human rights and the dignity of human nature at their core. This conclusion is based not only on foundational philosophical theories undergirding the rise of subjective rights but also the availability of protective vehicles already in place.

title: Impacts of Air Pollution on Diabetes Mortality Using Indonesian Forest Fires as an Instrument: Evidence from Transboundary Haze in Malaysia
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, University of Oxford - Health Economics Research Centre (HERC), affiliation not provided to SSRN, Clinical Trial Service Unit and Epidemiological Studies Unit, Nuffield Department of Population Health, University of Oxford, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Nanyang Technological University (NTU) - Asian School of the Environment, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Ministry of Health Malaysia, University of Malaya (UM) - Department of Medicine and University of Oxford - Health Economics Research Centre (HERC)

detail.title: Impacts of Air Pollution on Diabetes Mortality Using Indonesian Forest Fires as an Instrument: Evidence from Transboundary Haze in Malaysia
detail.abstract: Transboundary air pollution imposes substantial yet poorly quantified welfare costs on developing economies. This paper estimates the short-term causal impact of haze pollution on mortality among Malaysia’s population with diabetes—a group particularly vulnerable to environmental stressors. We combine daily air-quality data from 45 monitoring stations with mortality counts for 931,602 patients in the National Diabetes Registry. To address endogeneity between pollution and local economic activity, we exploit exogenous variation in particulate matter generated by satellite-observed Indonesian forest fires and prevailing wind direction in a two-stage Poisson instrumental-variable framework. Increases in particulate matter significantly raise mortality, with counterfactual analysis attributing 1,338–1,418 excess deaths among diabetes patients during 2017–2020 and welfare losses of 1.6–1.7 percent of total public-health expenditure. The findings highlight the sizable human-capital costs of transboundary environmental externalities in Southeast Asia and underscore the need for stronger regional cooperation on fire prevention and health protection.

title: Unicorn Trends: Value, Entry/Exit, Geography, and Aging
affiliations: University of Colorado at Denver - Department of Finance

detail.title: Unicorn Trends: Value, Entry/Exit, Geography, and Aging
detail.abstract: We analyze global unicorn trends from 2019 to 2025 using annual snapshots from the Hurun Global Unicorn Index. Four patterns stand out. First, counts and valuations expanded sharply but unevenly: after a hyper-creation year in 2021, growth slowed in 2022-2023 and rebounded in 2025 via valuation repricing; by 2025 the global stock reached 1,523 with aggregate value near US$5.6T. Second, flows show a boom-bust cycle: entries were concentrated in one year, while exits were dominated by valuation demotions rather than IPOs/M&A, reflecting tighter public markets. Third, geography broadened, with many more countries and cities hosting unicorns. Fourth, unicorns "aged in place" and founders were modestly older, consistent with lower exit hazards and a tilt toward capital-intensive sectors. An AR(1) on global counts indicates high persistence (≈0.78), a shock half-life of ~2-3 years, and an implied steady state above 2025 levels-signaling sticky momentum and headroom. These trends inform the shift toward venture-led capital formation and strategic investing.

title: Women transforming Financial Services in the United Arab Emirates
affiliations: Heriot-Watt University Edinburgh and University of London - Royal Holloway

detail.title: Women transforming Financial Services in the United Arab Emirates
detail.abstract: This report, a collaboration between Grant Thornton UAE and Heriot-Watt University Dubai, explores the evolving landscape of women’s leadership in the UAE’s financial services sector. Analysing 73 listed financial institutions, the study highlights both progress and persistent gaps in gender representation, particularly in critical governance roles such as Chief Risk Officer (CRO) and Head of Internal Audit (HIA). While women now occupy 15.8% of board seats, their presence in CRO (6%) and HIA (10%) roles remains limited, with eight institutions having no women on their boards. The report situates these findings within the broader context of the UAE’s economic diversification and ambitious national strategies, including Emiratisation and fintech innovation. Through interviews with senior women leaders, the report illuminates the challenges and opportunities facing women in risk, audit, and compliance, emphasising the importance of inclusive talent pipelines and supportive organisational cultures. The authors call for continued efforts to strengthen diversity at all levels, arguing that a richly diverse leadership is essential for the sector’s resilience and the nation’s long-term ambitions. This evidence-based analysis aims to inform policy, inspire dialogue, and catalyze action towards greater gender equity in UAE financial services.

title: The Autonomy Paradox: AI, Runaway Monopolization, and the Optimal Taxation of Capital

detail.title: The Autonomy Paradox: AI, Runaway Monopolization, and the Optimal Taxation of Capital
detail.abstract: This paper develops a dynamic equilibrium model to analyze the economic consequences of self-improving, autonomous capital-i.e. AI. I propose a paradigm shift where the classical principal-agent problem is driven away by a competition between principals and autonomous capital. The agent´s incentive and participation constraint vanish due to fierce competition with a new, super productive autonomous capital. Thus the agent´s effort is only determined by a new constraint-the survival constraint. If AI productivity surpasses that of humans agents drop out of the market. Former principals become now agents producing goods with autonomous capital. Due to potential non diminishing returns to scale at a certain point these new agents can not compete with even larger companys. A runaway to monopolization takes place. Hence the theoretical model features endogenous growth driven by capital accumulation with potentially non-diminishing returns, leading to runaway monopolization where large firms grow faster than small ones. This concentration, coupled with the erosion of labor's marginal product due to more and more productive autonomous capital, threatens to spur mass unemployment below a socially-defined survival consumption level. I characterize the government's problem of designing an optimal profit tax that redistributes income to ensure survival, while internalizing the tax's negative effect on investment and long-run growth. Using full dynamic optimization and numerical methods calibrated to OECD data, I derive the optimal tax path and identify precise technological conditions for runaway monopolization. The framework provides a unified basis for antitrust, redistribution, and growth policy in the age of AI, with extensions addressing political economy, international tax competition, and robustness.

detail.abstract: This study reassesses social mobility in late imperial China using genealogical records from 1,608 metropolitan examination candidates (1799-1904) across 18 provinces. Despite the celebrated meritocratic examination system, elite families successfully maintained advantages across multiple generations through mechanisms invisible to standard analyses. While the observable intergenerational correlation of 0.37 appears moderate, latent factor modeling reveals underlying family endowments transmitted at 0.58-57 percent higher. We directly test and reject the Markov assumption: observed three-and four-generation correlations (0.26, 0.144) exceed Markovian predictions (0.14, 0.052) by 86 percent and 177 percent, demonstrating that conventional two-generation analyses systematically underestimate persistence. Distinguishing educational from occupational mobility reveals the mechanism: examinations enabled educational advancement, but elite families uniquely converted credentials into positions through unavailable resources. Imperial China exhibited moderate average mobility but high elite closure-meritocratic selection coexisting with persistent stratification.
